meta.subtitle: Foodservice distributor compounding per-share earnings through independent-restaurant gains and buybacks, carried on rising debt

analystCommentary: We rate US Foods Holding a HOLD with a $98 to $118 target range against a current price of $93.72. Our probability-weighted fair value is $105.20, an expected upside of 12.2% against a bear-case downside of 25.3%, for a reward/risk of 0.48x, just under the 0.50x a BUY needs. The call is close, and the valuation section argues the deciding weight. This republish moves the label from BUY to HOLD. Operations are strong: in Q2'26 (the quarter ended June 27, 2026) net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, independent-restaurant case volume grew 5.1% and Adjusted EBITDA rose 10.2% to $604 million, and on August 6, 2026 management reaffirmed its FY26 guidance. What changed is the balance-sheet read. The corrected summary data carry a total-debt line: $5.2 billion at FY25, up from $4.7 billion at FY23, with cash and short-term investments rounding to $0.0 billion. Net debt is 3.0x trailing EBITDA on the page's measure, against the 2.6x the company reports on Adjusted EBITDA. With no cash buffer behind that debt, a stall in earnings would hit the equity harder, and the Bear is priced on that story.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: US Foods Holding Corp. markets, sells and distributes fresh, frozen and dry food and non-food products to foodservice customers in the United States, including independent and chain restaurants, healthcare, hospitality, government and education customers. Per its Q2'26 10-Q, it supplies approximately 250,000 customer locations and manages the business as a single operating segment. FY25 revenue was $39.4 billion, up 4.1%, and FY25 net income was $676 million. The company also provides MOXe, an all-in-one foodservice business application. It was incorporated in 2007 and is headquartered in Rosemont, Illinois.

thesis.body: US Foods is compounding per-share earnings through volume gains with independent restaurants, margin expansion and buybacks, and Q2'26 showed that model working. The counterweights are a first-half Adjusted EBITDA pace that trails the low end of full-year guidance, debt that has risen while buybacks continued, and an industry the 10-K describes as low-margin with very low switching costs. At 19.6x forward earnings, our Base already assumes the consensus earnings path, and the Bear is deep because leverage sits on a balance sheet with almost no cash. Expected upside of 12.2% clears the BUY bar; reward/risk of 0.48x narrowly misses it, so the derived label is HOLD.

catalysts: Independent-restaurant volume: case growth of 5.1% in Q2'26 ran well ahead of total case growth of 1.9%; the moat and growth sections carry the argument.
Second-half delivery against reaffirmed FY26 guidance, which includes a 53rd week; the income commentary sets out the half-year gap.
Buybacks: $640 million remained under the November 2025 authorization at the end of Q2'26.
Margin: Adjusted EBITDA margin rose 29 basis points year over year in Q2'26.
risks: Consumer demand: the 10-K (February 12, 2026) opens its business risks with spending on food prepared away from home.
Leverage: net debt of 3.0x trailing EBITDA with almost no cash leaves little room to absorb a profit shock.
Thin margins: cost inflation, deflation or a lag in passing costs through can move profits sharply.
Competition: the 10-K describes switching costs and barriers to entry as very low.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Q2'26 net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, which the company attributes to case-volume growth and food-cost inflation of 2.3%; total case volume rose 1.9%. Gross profit rose 8.0% to $1.9 billion, or 18.2% of sales, which the company credits to higher volume, improved cost of goods sold and a $19 million favorable year-over-year LIFO adjustment. Operating expenses grew 5.1%, slower than gross profit, and operating income reached $443 million, a 4.2% margin. Net income rose 22.8% to $275 million and GAAP diluted EPS rose 29.2% to $1.24. On the company's adjusted measures, Adjusted EBITDA rose 10.2% to $604 million at a 5.7% margin and Adjusted Diluted EPS rose 21.0% to $1.44.

The half-year is less even. For the 26 weeks ended June 27, 2026, Adjusted EBITDA rose from $937 million to $1,017 million, a pace just below the low end of the full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance set out next, and gross profit absorbed $33 million of LIFO expense. The FY26 guidance, first given on February 12, 2026 and reaffirmed on August 6, calls for 4% to 6% net-sales growth, 9% to 13% Adjusted EBITDA growth and 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth, including a 53rd week the company expects to add approximately 1% to Adjusted EBITDA growth. Both half-year periods have the same number of weeks, so that extra week is not in the comparison, and the second half has to carry the acceleration.

On the annual series, FY25 revenue was $39.4 billion, up 4.1%, at a gross margin of 17.4% and an operating margin of 3.0%, and FY25 GAAP diluted EPS was $2.94. The 2026 proxy (April 2, 2026) gives FY25 Adjusted Diluted EPS of $3.98, the base from which the company's EPS guidance grows. We use the GAAP series for history and the adjusted figure only to read the guidance. Consensus EPS of $4.78 for FY26E and $5.55 for FY27E sits far above the GAAP history; the pack does not state the basis of those estimates, and we use them as given.
financials.balanceCommentary:
Leverage is the main correction in this republish. Total debt rose from $4.7 billion at FY23 to $4.9 billion at FY24 and $5.2 billion at FY25. Cash and short-term investments fell from $0.3 billion to $0.0 billion in the rounded table over the same years, so net debt rose from $4.4 billion to the same level as total debt. On a trailing basis, net debt was 3.0x EBITDA and interest coverage was 4.1x; net interest expense was $77 million in Q2'26.

The August 6 release reports Net Debt at that same level at the end of Q2'26 and a ratio of Net Debt to Adjusted EBITDA of 2.6x, down from 2.7x at the end of FY25. The two net-debt figures agree. The ratios differ in the denominator: the company divides by Adjusted EBITDA, which adds back share-based compensation, LIFO reserve adjustments, restructuring charges and business transformation costs, while the page's ratio uses EBITDA before those adjustments. FY25 shows the size of the gap, with EBITDA of $1.7 billion in the summary table and Adjusted EBITDA of $1.932 billion in the proxy. We use the page's ratio as the stricter measure and treat the company's as the figure management manages to.

The ratio held steady because EBITDA grew, from $1.4 billion in FY23 to the FY25 level above, not because debt fell. Total equity declined to $4.3 billion at FY25 from a higher FY23 level as repurchases returned capital, and the current ratio fell to 1.16 at FY25 and 1.14 on a trailing basis. That interest coverage is serviceable while EBITDA grows. The exposure is the combination of a profit stall with no cash buffer, and that is how the Bear is priced.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is steady. FY25 free cash flow was $959 million after capital expenditure of $410 million, a 2.4% FCF margin, and the trailing FCF yield is 4.7%. Year to date through June 27, 2026, operating cash flow was $725 million, the same as a year earlier; the company explains that higher net income was offset by favorable changes in operating assets and liabilities in the prior-year period. First-half capital expenditure of $174 million went to information technology, property and equipment and distribution facilities, and free cash flow was $552 million against $569 million a year earlier. The company pays no dividend, and free cash flow has gone to buybacks rather than debt reduction, a choice the capital allocation section weighs.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $93.72 the shares trade at 28.8x trailing earnings, 0.5x sales and 14.7x trailing EV/EBITDA, the last of which counts the $5.2 billion of net debt. On consensus estimates the P/E falls to 19.6x next-twelve-months and ~16.9x FY27E. The drop from trailing to forward multiples reflects the earnings growth consensus expects and may also reflect a basis difference between the GAAP history and the estimates, which the pack does not label. The pack carries no peer multiples, so we value the shares on their own forward earnings, anchoring each scenario to a consensus EPS figure and a stated multiple. The shares sit between the $69.88 low and the $111.42 high of their 52-week range. The page's price history shows a sharp fall after the August 6 results: the shares traded near the top of that range in late August and dropped to around today's level by mid-September, with the steepest one-day fall in the second week of September. No source in the pack explains the decline, and we do not supply a reason; the Base inherits that move rather than any change in the reported numbers.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Independent-restaurant volume growth holds near Q2'26's pace, FY26 lands at the top of the 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS guidance, FY27 earnings run ahead of consensus, and the multiple re-rates above today's forward level. Implied $125, between the $120.00 median and the $130.00 top analyst target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Volume and margin gains continue at a slower pace, FY27 EPS meets the $5.55 consensus, and the shares hold today's 19.6x forward multiple on that figure. Implied $109, below the $116.67 consensus target and the $111.42 52-week high.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A consumer pullback cuts food-away-from-home volumes, cost deflation or a pass-through lag squeezes the thin margin, and EPS stalls near the FY26E $4.78 instead of growing into FY27. With net debt at 3.0x trailing EBITDA and no cash buffer, the multiple on that stalled figure compresses to below 15x. Implied $70, at the $69.88 52-week low and above the $65.00 lowest analyst target.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
Weighting Bull at 25%, Base at 55% and Bear at 20% gives weighted values of $31.25, $59.95 and $14.00 and a fair value of $105.20. Expected upside is 12.2%, bear-case downside is 25.3% and reward/risk is 0.48x. Expected upside clears the +10.0% BUY threshold, but reward/risk falls just short of 0.50x, so the derived label is HOLD.

The call is close. Moving five points of weight from Base to Bull would derive BUY, and so would a close only slightly below the current price on these scenarios. Several closes in the second half of September sat that low and derive BUY on the same scenarios, the late-August closes derive HOLD, and closes near the 52-week high would derive SELL, so the label depends on where the recent decline settles. The deciding split is the Bull weight. For a higher Bull weight: independent-restaurant volume accelerated in Q2'26, Adjusted EBITDA growth reached 10.2% in the quarter, management reaffirmed guidance, and 12 of 15 analysts rate the shares Buy. Against it: first-half Adjusted EBITDA growth ran below the guidance range, first-half free cash flow was lower than a year earlier, and the Bull needs both an earnings beat and a higher multiple. We keep the Bull weight at the lower setting; that is a judgment, not a finding.

The Bear weight rests on the Bear's own story. A consumer pullback within the next year is possible, but on August 6 the CEO described a "challenging but stable industry environment" and Q2'26 volumes accelerated, so we do not make it the central case. If it comes, the debt load means equity holders absorb the hit with no cash cushion, which is why the Bear sits at the 52-week low rather than at a shallower discount. The Base sits below the $116.67 consensus target because it holds today's multiple rather than expanding it.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: US Foods manages its business as a single operating segment, a broadline distributor serving approximately 250,000 customer locations through more than 70 distribution facilities, a fleet of over 6,500 trucks and over 90 cash and carry locations, per the Q2'26 10-Q. In Q2'26 total case volume grew 1.9%: independent-restaurant volume rose 5.1%, healthcare 3.5% and hospitality 4.4%, partially offset by a 1.5% decrease in chain volume. The offer to customers rests on Exclusive Brands, the MOX business platform and the Pronto delivery program, supported by over 4,000 sales associates.

moatFactors.name: National scale and network
moatFactors.body: The network lets the company, in its words, leverage its "nationwide scale and footprint while executing locally." The 10-K tempers that: certain competitors may have greater scale in certain markets, and regional and local distributors may have a lower cost to serve due to geographic proximity. Scale is an advantage against small rivals, not a barrier to them.

moatFactors.name: Exclusive Brands and MOX
moatFactors.body: The company says its customer relationships are further strengthened by the MOX digital platform, which helps customers manage orders and inventories, and it leads its customer promise with the Exclusive Brands portfolio. Gross margin rose from 16.1% in FY22 to 17.4% in FY25 and 17.6% on a trailing basis, consistent with a better mix, though no source ties the gain to these programs.

moatFactors.name: Low switching costs
moatFactors.body: The 10-K states that "the cost of switching distributors is very low, as are the barriers to entry," that the company generally does not have exclusive distribution agreements with customers, and that it competes with national, regional and local distributors, cash-and-carry operations, warehouse clubs and online wholesalers. That caps pricing power and is the main reason the moat is narrow.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow. Scale, a national network and the company's own brands and tools give US Foods a cost and service edge, and Q2'26 shows it adding volume in the channels it targets. By the 10-K's own account, though, customers can switch cheaply and entry barriers are very low, so the edge has to be re-earned through service and price rather than held through lock-in. Durability is therefore an execution question, and an operating margin of 3.0% in FY25 and 3.1% on a trailing basis leaves little room for error.

points: Independent restaurants: organic independent case volume rose 5.0% in Q2'26 and 4.7% over the 26 weeks, against total organic volume growth of 1.7% and 1.4%. Sustaining that gap is the core of the growth case.

Plan delivery: the CEO said Q2'26 results, including 10% Adjusted EBITDA growth and 21% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth, were "in line with our long-range plan." The proxy called 2025 a strong start to that three-year plan; the first-half pace is the open test.
Top line: consensus revenue of ~$41.5B for FY26E (+5%) and $43.2B for FY27E assumes mid-single-digit growth continues, consistent with the 4% to 6% FY26 guidance, which includes a 53rd week.
Per-share growth: consensus EPS rises from $4.78 for FY26E to $5.55 for FY27E, faster than revenue, which requires continued margin gains and a shrinking share count.

management.leadership: Per the 2026 proxy, filed April 2, 2026, the fiscal 2025 named executive officers were David E. Flitman, Chief Executive Officer; Dirk J. Locascio, Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer; Steven M. Guberman, Executive Vice President, Chief Transformation Officer and Nationally Managed Business; Randy J. Taylor, Executive Vice President, Field Operations and Local Sales; and John A. Tonnison, Executive Vice President, Chief Information and Digital Officer. The August 6, 2026 release identifies Mr. Flitman as Chair of the Board and CEO. Management frames its results against a three-year long-range plan, and the growth section weighs how far the record supports that framing.
management.capitalAllocation: US Foods pays no dividend and returns cash through buybacks. It repurchased $926 million of stock in FY25 and, over the 26 weeks ended June 27, 2026, 5.8 million shares for approximately $500 million, including 4.4 million shares for $374 million in Q2'26; $640 million remained under the November 2025 authorization. The cover-page share count of 216.33M is below the count at the March 18, 2026 proxy record date. Across FY24 and FY25, repurchases ran at about the level of free cash flow while total debt rose and cash ran down, so no free cash flow went to debt reduction; the summary table does not show what the added debt funded. On August 6 the CFO said the company is "maintaining our net leverage at 2.6 times." That is accurate on the Adjusted EBITDA basis, but holding the ratio flat means debt grows with EBITDA. It is a sound choice for per-share compounding while profits grow and an uncomfortable one if they stall. Per the proxy, the FY25 annual incentive plan weighted Adjusted EBITDA at 70%, distribution cost per case at 15% and "IND Market Share" at 15%.
management.governance: The captured proxy excerpt covers pay, ownership and the related-party policy, not board composition, so we do not assess board independence. The Chair and CEO roles are combined in Mr. Flitman, per the August 6 release. Per the 2026 proxy, Say-on-Pay received 96% approval in the prior year's vote, the Compensation and Human Capital Committee kept the FY25 incentive design similar to FY24, and Mr. Flitman's base salary rose 7.7% to $1,400,000 effective January 1, 2025. The Audit Committee reviews related-party transactions under a written policy. Because Adjusted EBITDA excludes share-based compensation and LIFO effects, the main pay metric rewards a measure that sits above GAAP earnings. For outside holders the record is orderly rather than distinctive.
management.insiderOwnership: As of the March 18, 2026 record date, per the 2026 proxy, directors and executive officers as a group (17 people) held 1,627,541 shares, less than 1% of the 220,242,295 outstanding, and Mr. Flitman held 319,221 shares. Six institutions reported stakes above 5%: The Vanguard Group (11.0%), Blackrock (8.8%), Boston Partners (7.0%), FMR LLC (6.9%), Wellington Management Group LLP (5.8%) and Capital World Investors (5.3%). The Vanguard figure rests on a Schedule 13G amendment as of November 29, 2024 and the Blackrock figure on a Schedule 13G as of December 31, 2023, so both may be out of date; the excerpt does not carry the dates behind the other four. No holder approaches control, so outside holders face no dominant shareholder, and alignment rests on pay design rather than on insider stakes, which are small.

idiosyncratic: Demand: the 10-K opens its business risks with consumer spending on food prepared away from home, which an economic downturn may reduce. Chain volume already fell in Q2'26, offset by gains in other channels. A broad volume decline is the Bear's trigger.

Margin sensitivity: the 10-K says profit levels may be negatively affected during product cost deflation even when the gross profit percentage stays constant, and rapid inflation may reduce margins if there is a lag in passing costs on. With FY25 operating margin of 3.0%, small cost moves reach earnings quickly.

Debt: the release's forward-looking statements list the level of interest rates, the availability of indebtedness and restrictions under the agreements governing it among the factors that could affect results. With the leverage and thin cash set out in the balance sheet commentary, a profit stall would push the ratio up quickly.
Structural demand: the release's forward-looking statements name advancements in pharmaceutical therapies as a factor that may reduce the consumption of food prepared away from home.
risks.systemic: The 10-K describes U.S. foodservice distribution as sensitive to national, regional and local economic conditions, and cites tariffs, trade policies, inflationary pressure and supply chain disruptions among the factors that could weigh on consumer confidence and discretionary spending. Because the business runs on high volume and low margin, a shock to consumer spending or input costs reaches earnings quickly. Interest rates matter through the cost and availability of debt and through the multiple the market pays for a leveraged, low-margin earner.

body: We rate US Foods Holding a HOLD with a $98 to $118 target range around a fair value of $105.20. The business is executing: Q2'26 grew volume, margin and earnings, and management reaffirmed FY26 guidance. At 19.6x forward earnings our Base already assumes the consensus path, and leverage on a balance sheet with almost no cash makes the Bear deep enough that reward/risk lands at 0.48x, just short of a BUY.

On unchanged scenarios, BUY derives at any close slightly below today's $93.72, and SELL derives only near the $111.42 52-week high. On the evidence, we would raise the Bull weight, and with it move to BUY, if second-half results put FY26 Adjusted EBITDA growth inside the 9% to 13% guidance range while independent-restaurant volume growth holds near its Q2'26 pace. We would raise the Bear weight and lower our fair value if total case volume turns negative or net debt rises faster than EBITDA.
